summary: To stop people from impersonating telephone numbers, there must be a way to prove who has authority over a number. This document describes how X.509 certificates can be used for that purpose, as one part of the broader STIR architecture for authenticated calling.

eli5.summary: It is like an official ID card for phone numbers. Only the number's real owner gets the card, so a fake caller cannot show one.

questions: how do certificates prove ownership of a phone number
how do certificates prove phone number ownership
what is the tn authorization list
how to stop caller id spoofing
subtitle: How X.509 certificates can prove that a caller is allowed to use a telephone number.

tldr.problem: Robocallers and other attackers impersonate calling numbers, and nothing cryptographically shows who has authority over a telephone number.
tldr.mechanism: Certificates assert that authority, either through the certificate subject or through a new TN Authorization List extension that lists numbers, ranges or service provider codes. A second extension, JWT Claim Constraints, limits what a signer may put in a PASSporT.
tldr.outcome: It gives STIR a credential system that verifiers can use to check a caller's signature. Certificate freshness is left for further study. A later RFC, RFC 9118, updates it.

facts.label: Required signature algorithms
facts.value: ECDSA P-256 and RSA PKCS #1 v1.5

today: RFC 8226 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9118, so read the two together. It supplies the certificate side of the STIR design in RFC 8224.

sections.title: Impersonation and the Need for Credentials
sections.content:
The STIR problem statement (RFC 7340) names the ability to impersonate a calling party number as the primary enabler of robocalling, vishing (voicemail hacking), swatting and related attacks. Robocallers want to appear to call from some number, any number, but prefer not to use one that traces back to them, so they impersonate numbers not assigned to them.

A key part of the fix is a credential that identifies who controls a telephone number. This document builds one on X.509 version 3 certificates (RFC 5280) and adds a Telephony Number Authorization List extension. It is written for the STIR in-band architecture of RFC 8224, where an authentication service signs and a verification service checks, but it could serve other protocols too.

The RFC specifies only the credential syntax and semantics. It assumes no particular CA or deployment, and expects that deployment experience will be needed to settle operational models.
sections.eli5: Scammers pretend to call from a phone number that is not theirs. To stop that, a number needs a kind of ID card that only its real owner can show.

sections.title: Two Ways to Show Authority
sections.content:
The RFC describes two approaches that are not mutually exclusive. In the first, the certificate subject itself says who the holder is. The subject might be a domain name in the subjectAltName that relying parties know as a carrier, or a Service Provider Code such as an Operating Company Number (OCN) or Service Provider Identifier (SPID). A relying party then uses an outside data set or a trust relationship with peer carriers to decide whether that carrier controls a number.

In the second, the certificate carries a new TN Authorization List naming the telephone numbers it covers. The list can be a literal value in the certificate or a network service that verifiers query. This suits cases where the certificate owner would prefer, for privacy reasons, not to be identified.

The signing format in RFC 8224 is the same either way. Only the verifier's authorization decision changes.
sections.eli5: You can prove a phone number is yours by showing a company badge that everyone trusts, or by showing a list that names your exact numbers. Either way the call is signed the same way.

sections.title: Certificate Requirements for STIR
sections.content:
RFC 8224 requires each credential system to answer several questions, and this RFC answers them. The URI schemes permitted in the Identity header info parameter are HTTP, CID and SIP. No special procedures are needed beyond dereferencing that URI.

On algorithms, implementations MUST support both ECDSA with the P-256 curve and RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 for certificate signatures. RSA is mandated only as a transitional mechanism because of its widespread use in existing PKIs, and the RFC expects it will eventually be deprecated. Certificates MUST also provide keying material sufficient for ECDSA with P-256 and SHA-256 signatures, the ES256 signatures required by PASSporT (RFC 8225).

Verifiers can get certificates by value in a SIP request (for example in a multipart MIME body referenced by a CID URI), or by dereferencing the info URI. Implementations are REQUIRED to support SIP (via SUBSCRIBE/NOTIFY), HTTP and HTTPS for that.
sections.eli5: The certificate has to work with the signing method the call system uses. Two kinds of digital signature must be supported, and the certificate can be sent with the call or fetched from a web address.

sections.title: Enrollment and Delegation
sections.content:
For the TN Authorization List, the RFC covers three enrollment models.

  • Top-down: the CA works with national numbering authorities and issues credentials to those who are assigned numbers. The RFC uses the United States as an example, where blocks go to Local Exchange Carriers (LECs) through NANPA.
  • Bottom-up: the CA requires proof of control, either automated (such as texting a URL to the number) or a manual administrative process.
  • Delegation: a certificate holder passes some or all authority to another party, possibly through several levels. The RFC warns that lengthy delegation chains are brittle and can delay verification.

Keys are held by whichever entity signs. For a single-number end user certificate it might be the device; for a big provider, an intermediary. The RFC RECOMMENDS distributing private keys as PKCS #8 objects signed by a trusted entity, for example in the CMS package of RFC 5958.
sections.eli5: There are three ways to get a number ID card: the phone-number authority hands it out, you prove you can receive a text at that number, or the owner lets someone else use some of their numbers.

sections.title: The TN Authorization List
sections.content:
The extension is non-critical and uses the object identifier id-pe-TNAuthList, { id-pe 26 }. It is a sequence of entries, each one of three choices:

  • spc: a Service Provider Code, which indirectly names all numbers of that provider.
  • range: a starting TelephoneNumber plus a count of at least 2.
  • one: a single TelephoneNumber, an IA5String of 1 to 15 characters drawn from digits, star and pound.

The count only applies to start numbers that contain no star or pound characters, and adding it MUST NOT make the number longer. For example, start 10 with count 91 is invalid. In an end-entity certificate the list shows the numbers authorized; in a CA certificate it limits the numbers for certification paths through it.

A separate extension, JWT Claim Constraints (id-pe-JWTClaimConstraints, { id-pe 27 }), is optional and non-critical. Its mustInclude field names claims that must appear in addition to iat, orig and dest, and permittedValues restricts a claim to listed values.
sections.eli5: The list says which numbers the certificate covers: a whole company, a block of numbers in a row, or one number. A second small note can say what extra things the signer must or must not write on a call.

sections.title: Freshness, Revocation and Lists by Reference
sections.content:
Numbers move between owners, for example through number portability, so a verifier must check not only that a certificate is valid but also that its scope still contains the number. Two options are named: rely on short-lived certificates and skip status checks, or use status information from the authority such as OCSP. The first puts the burden on enrollment, the second on verification. The RFC makes no recommendation and says this needs further study and implementation experience.

For providers with huge numbers of telephone numbers, the list can be given by reference. A new Authority Information Access method, id-ad-stirTNList ({ id-ad 14 }), points to an HTTPS URI. Dereferencing it returns the complete DER-encoded list with the content type application/tnauthlist. Verifiers MUST support the AIA extension.
sections.eli5: Phone numbers can change hands, so a verifier has to make sure the ID card is still current. It can use cards that expire quickly, or ask the issuer. Big companies can put a web link on the card instead of the whole list.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is entirely about security, and points to RFC 5280 for general certificate security. Its own concern is privacy: a list in a certificate can reveal numbers unrelated to the call being checked, and linking thousands of numbers to a certificate through AIA makes this worse. Even an SPC can tie a certificate to a carrier and, with industry databases, to its numbers. One suggested mitigation is short-lived certificates for individual numbers.

The list fetched by reference travels over HTTPS, so it is protected in transit. It is not a signed object, however, so the server must be trusted to return the list faithfully. Online status checks can also disclose private information if precautions are not taken.
sections.eli5: A big list of numbers on a card could tell strangers more than they need to know. Using many small cards, or protecting the list when it is sent, helps keep things private.

viz.caption: CHOICES IN A TN AUTHORIZATION LIST ENTRY

items.label: ServiceProviderCode
items.desc: An IA5String naming a service provider, such as an OCN or SPID.

items.label: TelephoneNumberRange
items.desc: A start number and a count of at least 2.

items.label: TelephoneNumber
items.desc: A single number of 1 to 15 characters from 0123456789#*.
